items.title: Expected waiting time until a pattern first appears
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** The candidate is handed a stream of independent trials and asked for the
expected number of trials until a short target pattern shows up for the first time —
a run of identical outcomes, or a named two- or three-symbol sequence.

**What it measures.** That the process is Markov in *how much of the target is currently
matched*, so the whole history collapses to a handful of states; that one-step
conditioning turns those states into a small linear system; and that a trial which
breaks the partial match resets to the correct state, which is rarely the state you
started in. Interviewers keep this one because a candidate who reasons from the marginal
probability alone lands nowhere near the truth, and because the standard follow-up —
compare two targets of equal length — instantly separates a memorised answer from an
understood structure.

**Typical realisations.** Expected trials until k consecutive successes on a biased
trial; expected flips until a named sequence; explaining why two equally likely patterns
have unequal waiting times.

items.title: Three gold tokens in a row
items.statement_md:
A kiosk hands out one token every time you press its button. Each press independently
produces a **gold** token with probability 1/3 and a **silver** token otherwise; nothing
the machine has already dispensed changes the odds on the next press.

You press repeatedly and stop at the exact moment your three most recent tokens are all
gold.

Give the expected number of presses, as an exact value. Set the calculation up explicitly
rather than quoting a formula, and say what each quantity you introduce stands for.

reasoning_rubric.description: Collapses the history to the length of the current gold run and says why that is sufficient — the next press does not care what came before the current streak.

levels.0: Works with the raw sequence or guesses from 1/(1/3)^3 = 27 with no state notion.
levels.1: Mentions 'states' but the set is wrong or unbounded (e.g. tracks total golds so far, not the current run).
levels.2: Correct states 0, 1, 2 with an absorbing state at 3, but does not justify why run length is the whole story.
levels.3: States 0, 1, 2 plus absorption, with an explicit statement that the run length is a sufficient statistic because presses are independent.

reasoning_rubric.description: Writes the one-step conditioning equations correctly, in particular that a silver token returns the process to a run of zero with no partial credit.

levels.0: No equations, or equations that omit the +1 for the press just spent.
levels.1: Equations written but the failure branch is wrong — e.g. a silver drops the run by one instead of clearing it.
levels.2: All three equations correct; the reset is right but stated without comment.
levels.3: All three equations correct, the full reset is called out as the point of the problem, and the +1 per press is justified as conditioning on the next trial.

reasoning_rubric.description: Solves the system to 39 and applies at least one independent check on the magnitude, rather than reporting whatever the algebra produced.

levels.0: Arithmetic error carried through with no check; answer far from 39.
levels.1: Reaches a number near 39 but cannot say whether it is plausible.
levels.2: Reaches 39 correctly with no sanity check offered.
levels.3: Reaches 39 and checks it — e.g. notes it must exceed 27 because resets waste presses, or recovers 3 + 3^2 + 3^3 as a telescoping pattern.

hints: Nothing about the next press depends on the entire history — only on one number describing where you currently stand. What is that number, and how many values can it take?
Let E_j be the expected number of further presses given that your current unbroken gold run has length j, for j = 0, 1, 2. Condition on the very next press.
A silver token does not shorten your run, it erases it: from any j you land back at E_0. Write those three equations and solve, or notice the answer comes out as 3 + 3^2 + 3^3.
follow_ups: Generalise: gold has probability p and you need a run of k. Give the closed form and check it reproduces your answer.

Same kiosk, but now you stop the first time a gold is immediately followed by a silver. Is that expectation larger or smaller than the run-of-three answer, and what is structurally different about the reset?
How would you get the variance of the number of presses, and would you expect it to be small or large relative to the mean here?

items.title: Fair value of a bounded keep-or-discard game
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** A game pays out the value of whichever draw the candidate chooses to keep.
There is a hard cap on the number of draws, a discarded draw is gone for good, and the
final draw is compulsory. The candidate is asked to price the game and to state the rule
they would follow at each decision point.

**What it measures.** Backward induction from the last stage; the realisation that every
earlier decision is a single comparison between the number in hand and one continuation
value; and arithmetic that survives being done aloud. Trading desks like it because the
output *is* a fair value, so the natural escalation is "now quote me a market on it",
which carries the identical reasoning into bid/offer language without a new problem.

**Typical realisations.** A die you may reroll a bounded number of times; a bounded
sequence of card or urn draws with the option to pass; a variant charging a fee per
discard, which shifts every threshold down.

sources.title: Jane Street Interview Guide: Mental Math, Probability, Trading Games

Useful because it places the pattern inside a described interview process, not a question list.

items.title: Pricing a three-roll die game with no recall
items.statement_md:
Here is a game. A fair ten-sided die, faces 1 through 10, is rolled where you can see it.
You may **bank** the face showing — that ends the game and pays you that many dollars — or
**discard** it and roll again. You get at most three rolls in total, and a discarded roll
is gone: you cannot return to it. If you reach the third roll you must bank whatever it
shows.

Assume you are after the largest expected payout available to you. What is the game worth
the moment before anything has been rolled? Give the exact fair value in dollars, and
state the rule you would follow at each point where you have a choice.

reasoning_rubric.description: Prices the game from the final compulsory roll backwards, rather than trying to reason forward from the first roll.

levels.0: Reasons forward or averages the three rolls; no notion of a continuation value.
levels.1: Says 'work backwards' but computes only one stage, or reuses 5.5 as the continuation value at both decisions.
levels.2: Both stages computed in the right order with the right values (5.5 then 6.75), stated without justification.
levels.3: Explicit backward chain — last roll is worth 5.5, that number is what a discard on roll two buys, and 6.75 is what a discard on roll one buys — with the recursion named.

reasoning_rubric.description: States the stopping rule at each decision as a comparison against that stage's continuation value, and gets both thresholds right.

levels.0: No rule given, or a fixed rule such as 'keep 6 only' applied at every stage.
levels.1: One threshold correct, the other wrong or absent; or thresholds given as numbers with no comparison principle behind them.
levels.2: Bank 7 or higher on the first roll, bank 6 or higher on the second — correct but asserted.
levels.3: Both thresholds correct AND derived as 'keep the face iff it beats what the remaining game is worth', with the boundary case (a face exactly equal to the continuation value) addressed as indifferent.

reasoning_rubric.description: Carries the stage arithmetic accurately to the exact fair value and offers a plausibility check on the number.

levels.0: Value materially wrong, or reported without units or exactness.
levels.1: Method sound but an arithmetic slip leaves the value off; error not noticed.
levels.3: Reaches 7.45 exactly and bounds it sensibly — above 6.75, below 10, and rising with each extra roll but by less each time.

hints: Start at the end. What is this game worth to you at the instant you are about to take your last, compulsory roll?
At every earlier point the only question is whether the number in front of you beats what you still hold if you throw it away. That 'what you still hold' is a single number per stage.
With one roll left the game is worth 5.5, so on the second roll you bank 6 and up. Work out what that makes the game worth with two rolls left, then apply the same test to the first roll.
follow_ups: Now each discard costs you 50 cents, paid whether or not you end up better off. Which way do the two thresholds move, and is the game still worth playing?
You have to quote a two-sided market on this game to someone who knows exactly what you know. Where do you put your bid and offer, and what determines the width?
Allow n rolls instead of three. What does the value tend to as n grows, and roughly how quickly does it get there?

items.title: Expected count over a random arrangement via indicators
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** The candidate is asked for the expected size of a count taken over a random
arrangement — matches, adjacencies, runs, records, fixed points — in a setting where the
individual contributions to that count are plainly not independent of one another.

**What it measures.** Writing the count as a sum of 0/1 contributions, getting one
contribution's probability by a symmetry argument rather than a calculation, and saying
out loud that adding expectations never required independence in the first place. The
dependence is the whole trap: candidates who go after the count's distribution run out of
time, and candidates who silently assume independence reach the right number for a wrong
reason — which the variance follow-up exposes immediately.

**Typical realisations.** Expected number of people handed back their own item after a
shuffle; expected count of neighbouring like or unlike pairs in a shuffled row; expected
number of distinct values observed.

sources.title: Probability Brainteasers for Quant Interviews: Dice, Coins, Cards, Urns
sources.evidence: A brainteaser taxonomy that names four tools it says the rounds actually test, two of which are the additivity of expectation and the use of 0/1 counters, and which asserts that several named market-making and hedge-fund loops lean on this family. Attests the technique, not merely one puzzle.

sources.title: Top 50 Quant Interview Questions (With Full Solutions)

sources.title: Quant Interview Questions 2026: 50 With Answers

items.title: Expected changeovers on a mixed parcel line
items.statement_md:
Twelve parcels travel down a conveyor in single file, in an order that is uniformly random
among all the orders they could arrive in. Four of the twelve are marked **express**; the
other eight are **standard**.

The sorter at the end of the belt has to flip its arm whenever two parcels that are next
to each other in the line carry different markings. Each such flip is one *changeover*.

How many changeovers should the operator expect over a run of twelve parcels? Give the
exact expectation, and be explicit about why your method is sound even though whether one
gap is a changeover clearly tells you something about its neighbour.

reasoning_rubric.description: Turns the count into a sum of one 0/1 variable per adjacent gap, and counts the gaps correctly.

levels.0: Attempts the distribution of the changeover count, or guesses.
levels.1: Mentions indicators but attaches them to parcels rather than to gaps, or uses 12 gaps instead of 11.
levels.2: Eleven gap indicators summed correctly, set up without comment.
levels.3: Eleven gap indicators, with the count-as-a-sum step named as the move that makes the problem tractable.

reasoning_rubric.description: Computes the probability that one particular gap is a changeover, by symmetry over the pair occupying that gap.

levels.0: Uses 4/12 x 8/12 or similar, treating the two slots as sampled with replacement.
levels.1: Right idea but only one ordering counted, giving 16/33 halved, or an off-by-one in the 11 denominator.
levels.3: Gets 16/33 and justifies it — the ordered pair in any fixed gap is uniform over ordered pairs of distinct parcels, so the gap's position is irrelevant.

reasoning_rubric.description: Says explicitly that summing expectations is valid here without any independence assumption, and does not smuggle one in.

levels.0: Asserts the gaps are independent, or multiplies probabilities as though they were.
levels.1: Adds the expectations without ever addressing dependence.
levels.2: Notes that expectation is additive regardless of dependence.
levels.3: Notes additivity holds regardless of dependence, and identifies concretely where the dependence lives — overlapping gaps share a parcel, so their indicators are correlated even though the means still add.

hints: You are being asked for the expected value of a count. Counts are sums of ones — find the things you are counting.
Attach a 0/1 variable to each of the eleven boundaries between neighbouring parcels. Then you only ever need the probability for a single boundary.

Fix any one boundary: the ordered pair of parcels sitting there is uniform over all ordered pairs of distinct parcels, so the chance they differ is 2 x 4 x 8 / (12 x 11). Multiply by 11 and you are done — no independence was ever needed.
follow_ups: Run the same twelve parcels around a closed loop instead of a straight line. What changes in the setup, and does the answer go up or down?
Which pairs of boundary indicators are correlated, and in which direction? Sketch how you would get the variance of the changeover count.
Keep the ratio but scale up: 40 express and 80 standard among 120 parcels. Roughly how many changeovers, and what is the limiting rate per gap?
